rationale: B wins because it turns the disclosed holes into assignable stories, not just launch wrappers. Its strongest line, "Replit's agent built our apps. Here is how many ran without a fix," gives a reporter a method, while A steps on its own foot with "You pay per build," a billing unit the update never supplied. A is useful, especially the reliability angle, but B is sharper about what must be proven before anyone pitches this with a straight face.
gaps_in_A: "You pay per build" is a made-up billing unit; the update only says pricing is usage-based on top of subscriptions.
"one English sentence" over-specifies the product claim; the source says plain-English description, not sentence-length magic.
"full chain a human developer would otherwise own" pushes beyond the facts; code, database, and deploy are given, but production-quality ownership is not.
"Replit is betting class on it" is cute but loose; the angle itself admits classroom use of the agent is unproven.
gaps_in_B: "tens of millions of hobbyists" turns a company-claimed platform-user number into a hobbyist audience the update never gave.
"the same product will land in the accounts schools already use" assumes education-account availability; the facts only say Replit is used heavily in education.
"would rather describe an app than code one" states user preference without evidence; the update only says Replit positions the agent for non-engineers and vibe coders.
"defensive-comment" is the wrong shape label for a reporter story; this is a pricing-risk or accountability angle, not a reactive comment.
